title: Geothermal leak causes lane closure on Main Street in Downtown Boise
summary: The Ada County Highway District says the lane restriction may be in place for several days while repairs are made, and drivers are asked to use an alternate route if possible.
text:
BOISE, Idaho — A geothermal leak is causing lane restrictions on Main Street in Downtown Boise.
Main St. has been reduced to one lane between 11th and 12th Streets so crews can address the issue.
The Ada County Highway District says the lane restriction may be in place for several days while repairs are made, and drivers are asked to use an alternate route if possible.

title: Four months into fiscal year, Idaho state revenues are $82.5 million above projections
summary: Through the first four months of fiscal year 2027, total Idaho state revenue collections are $82.5 million ahead of forecast, a new state report released last week shows. According to the October results posted in the new Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Monitor, the state is projected to end fiscal year 2027 in June with a […]
text:
Four months into fiscal year, Idaho state revenues are $82.5 million above projections
Idaho legislators to begin setting next year’s state budget in January
The Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Through the first four months of fiscal year 2027, total Idaho state revenue collections are $82.5 million ahead of forecast, a new state report released last week shows.
Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services
According to the October results posted in the new Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Monitor, the state is projected to end fiscal year 2027 in June with a positive ending balance of $688.3 million.
For the month of October itself, state revenues collections came in 1.9% below forecast. But year-to-date, state revenues are ahead of the forecast by 4.8%, the report shows.
The projected $688.3 million ending balance is an increase of almost $540 million compared to the ending balance Idaho state legislators estimated at the end of the 2026 legislative session.
“Things are looking positive,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chair of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. “I’m happy to see we are running a little ahead.”
Idaho runs on a fiscal year calendar that begins July 1 and ends June 30 each year. That means the October revenue report includes data from the first four months of fiscal year 2027.
    What do Idaho’s increased revenues mean for budget setting next year?
Idaho state legislators will begin working on setting the fiscal year 2028 budget once the new legislative session begins in January.
So far, this year’s revenue increases are a change compared to last year, when state legislators approved across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies and departments to pay for tax changes included in the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Grow’s committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, is responsible for setting the state budget, which is then sent to the full Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate for approval.
Grow said increased revenues could create new challenges for legislators during the upcoming legislative session.
“The challenge we have is when revenues look a little stronger, some may want to go back and undo the cuts, refill or replace the cuts that were made last session,” Grow said.
“I’ve been told before that when things are tight, it is more a little more understandable by departments and agencies that things are tight,” Grow said. “But when revenue seems to be strong, then we get a lot of (funding) requests.”
Grow said he doesn’t think the JFAC and the Idaho Legislature will reverse or backfill all of last year’s budget cuts this year.

title: Boise's Mathair Earth crafts handmade soap and skincare using plant-based ingredients
summary: 🧼 Kombucha, goat's milk, and even beer? That's what's inside the handmade soaps at Mathair Earth, a Boise mother-daughter business.
text:
BOISE BENCH, Idaho — On the Boise Bench, soaps, body care and skincare are all being made by hand by a mother and her daughters at Mathair Earth.
From kombucha to goat's milk — even beer — what goes into these bars of soap may surprise you.
Sahana Patel shares a look at the unique ingredients and story behind this Made in Idaho business:
"We've chosen to go plant-based. They're cruelty free, and they don't have any issues with hormones being added into it," Mariah Stricklin said.
Stricklin and her sister grew up watching their mom make soap at home after she started the business back in 2009.
"She's just always really liked handmade soap, and she's a creative. It's because handmade soap feels better than store-bought," Stricklin said.
What started at home now has its own storefront off Overland Road. After college, Stricklin and her sister joined their mom, helping grow Mathair Earth.
"It does feel nice to actually have a storefront that's complete, that looks fresh and clean, that represents the products well," Stricklin said.
Stricklin said there's a lot of science behind each batch — from getting the formula right, to mixing, curing and eventually stocking the shelves. She said about 95% of what they carry is made by them, right here in Idaho.
"Boise is great for supporting local in a different way. I think it's more meaningful to our community," Stricklin said.
Mathair Earth is located at 2436 W. Overland Rd, Boise, ID 83705.
The storefront is open Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, and you can shop online anytime on their website.

title: Mule deer buck tests positive for CWD in Idaho near Oregon border
summary: A mule deer buck that was killed by a hunter in Idaho along the Snake River near the border with Oregon has tested positive for chronic wasting disease, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said. The positive test marked the first time chronic wasting disease has been detected in Unit 13, which is located […]
text:
Mule deer buck tests positive for CWD in Idaho near Oregon border
First positive chronic wasting disease test reported in Idaho’s Unit 13 in Idaho County
Chronic wasting disease, or CWD, is a contagious, incurable and fatal neurological disease that can be transmitted between hooved mammals such as elk, moose and deer. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
A mule deer buck that was killed by a hunter in Idaho along the Snake River near the border with Oregon has tested positive for chronic wasting disease, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said.
The positive test marked the first time chronic wasting disease has been detected in Unit 13, which is located in Idaho County and is bordered by the Snake River on the west and the Salmon River on the east.
The location is about a half mile from the Oregon border, Idaho state officials said in a Wednesday press release.
Chronic wasting disease, or CWD, is a contagious, incurable and fatal neurological disease that can be transmitted between hooved mammals such as elk, moose and deer.
The disease was first detected in Idaho in 2021.
In announcing the positive CWD test, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said tissue samples provided by hunters help give state officials important insight into where the disease is occurring and how common it is.
“With the hunting season now concluded in Unit 13, we encourage the public to continue supporting CWD surveillance by reporting road-killed deer and elk, animals found dead, and animals exhibiting unusual behavior,” said Stacey Dauwalter, IDFG Wildlife Health Program coordinator. “These reports and samples are essential to helping us monitor the disease.”
Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said they have tested more than 3,500 elk and deer for chronic wasting disease so far this year.
The recent positive test for the mule deer buck killed near the Oregon border marked the first CWD detection outside units that have previously had elk and deer test positive for CWD, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said.
State officials said their priority is to keep the percentage of animals infected low so that big game populations will remain healthy. However, they said CWD cannot be eliminated because it remains in the environment for decades.
More information about chronic wasting disease is available on the Idaho Department of Fish and Game’s website.

text:
National outages, emergency alerts become fodder for doomsday conspiracy theories
Online speculation comes as country’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats
Cases of bottled water are displayed for sale at a Costco in Burbank, Calif. Doomsday conspiracy theories circulating online have fueled calls for Americans to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies amid unfounded predictions of widespread blackouts and other catastrophes. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days.
Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst.
The supposed warning signs? A nationwide flight shutdown, disruptions to banking and technology services and a routine federal emergency alert test — seemingly unrelated events that some online users portrayed as evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or impending emergency.
The doomsday predictions lack credible evidence. But the speculation comes as the nation’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats — raising legitimate questions about the country’s preparedness for major disruptions.
Federal officials have said they found no evidence that the latest disruptions were connected or that a nationwide emergency was imminent. And some emergency management experts warn that false alarms can undermine public trust in official warnings and complicate disaster response when real emergencies strike.
Still, the attention surrounding these unfounded predictions does not necessarily mean they have gained widespread acceptance.
Joseph Uscinski, a political science professor at the University of Miami who studies conspiracy theories, cautioned against interpreting viral posts as evidence of a broader shift in public beliefs.
“Your average conspiracy theory dies on the vine,” he said, noting that many fade as the news cycle moves on.
Uscinski described the reaction as a recurring pattern: A major event sparks conspiracy theories, those claims attract attention and then eventually fade, only for the cycle to repeat when another event captures the public’s attention.
Some of the latest rumors appeared to gain traction ahead of Tuesday’s nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which interrupted television and radio broadcasts across the country. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, and the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, had announced the Nov. 17 test in September as part of routine efforts to evaluate the nation’s emergency warning infrastructure. Federal rules require nationwide testing at least once every three years.

One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions […]
text:
Idahoans should know about the brazen new plan to sell our public lands
The US Department of Interior just released a strategic plan that, for the first time ever, prioritizes selling public land under its control, writes guest columnist Rob Mason.
The Lewis Clark National Historic Trail, as seen near the Lemhi Pass in Idaho. Today the pass is traversed by a 35-mile long graded unpaved Backcountry Byway through public lands where colorful wildflowers like arrowleaf balsam-root, lupine and delphinium rival the sunset. (Photo by Bob Wick/Bureau of Land Management)
This election season, public lands were on the ballot. The issue showed up in campaigns across the country, including here in Idaho where we reelected leaders who have made this position clear: Public lands are not for sale.
One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions are also smart politics. It’s not everyday that you see an issue with such broad bipartisan support all across the state.
New poll finds 96% Idaho voters say public lands should remain in public hands
We’re fortunate to have U.S. Congressman Mike Simpson and U.S. Sens. Jim Risch and Mike Crapo on our side as advocates for keeping public lands in public hands, because unfortunately the attacks on our outdoor heritage just don’t seem to be going away.
The latest example sadly comes directly from the U.S. Department of Interior, which just released a strategic plan that, for the first time ever, prioritizes selling public land under its control. Here in Idaho, that most likely means they could be selling off our treasured Bureau of Land Management lands.
Interior’s plan says the agency will “work to decrease the size of the federal estate.” In other words, it plans to sell our public lands. Its approach is not a narrow, targeted one meant to solve a specific local problem, where transferring a small piece of public land to a local government might make sense from time to time.
Instead, this Department of the Interior appears intent on trying to sell off as much of our public land as it can. There’s no acreage limit, no ceiling on how much public land could be sold, and no endpoint for the sell-off.
The plan calls for public lands to be sold to state and local governments, but those governments are unlikely to be able to afford the long-term costs of land management and will be forced to find a way to make a profit from the land. Ultimately that means many of those formerly-public lands will be privatized, commercialized, or both. Think data center developers aren’t paying attention to this?
At a time when Americans are rightly up in arms about the rapid, irresponsible construction of data centers, it’s hard to understand why the administration would pursue a policy that could allow them to be built even faster by selling BLM lands that may ultimately end up in the hands of data center developers.
